metadata.description: Learn common changes that may occur in the last days and hours of life, how families can offer comfort and when to contact healthcare or hospice professionals.
metadata.title: 10 Signs The End May Be Near

landing.title: 10 Signs The End May Be Near
landing.intro: Families often notice the same changes as someone approaches the end of life. Here are 10 signs to know.

disclaimer: General educational information about expected dying only. These changes do not prove that a person is close to death and must be interpreted by their healthcare or hospice team. Sudden collapse, severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, stroke signs, heavy bleeding, a seizure or unresponsiveness in someone not expected to be dying requires immediate emergency help.

sections.title: 10 Signs Someone May Be In The Last Days Of Life
sections.intro: These changes are most meaningful when a healthcare team already expects that someone is dying. No single sign can predict the exact time, and not everyone experiences every change.

points.title: Sleeping much more
paragraphs: The person may become increasingly drowsy, spend most of the day asleep and move in and out of consciousness. They may respond slowly or stop responding even though they may still be aware of familiar voices.

points.title: Profound weakness
paragraphs: Standing, walking, washing or changing position may become difficult or impossible. The person may remain in bed and need much more help because the body has very little energy.

points.title: Little interest in food or drink
paragraphs: Appetite and thirst commonly fall as the body slows down. Families should not force food or fluid; the care team can suggest mouth care, safe sips or other ways to ease dryness.

points.title: Difficulty swallowing
paragraphs: Tablets, food and drinks may become hard to swallow. Tell the healthcare team, because medicines may need to be changed to another form and unsafe feeding can cause choking or aspiration.

points.title: Irregular breathing or long pauses
paragraphs: Breathing may alternate between shallow and deeper breaths, become slower or include pauses. This can be distressing to witness, but the person may not experience it in the same way observers do.

points.title: Noisy breathing
paragraphs: Saliva or mucus can collect when someone is too weak to cough or swallow effectively, creating a rattling sound. Repositioning and medicines may help, so contact the care team for guidance.

points.title: Confusion, restlessness or unusual experiences
paragraphs: The person may not recognise people or places, speak to someone others cannot see, pick at bedding or try to get up. Pain, medicines, infection or chemical changes can contribute and should be assessed.

points.title: Cold, pale, blue or mottled skin
paragraphs: Hands and feet may become cool as circulation changes. Skin can look pale, bluish or patchy, with colour changes sometimes easier to see around the lips, mouth, ears, knees or feet.

points.title: Passing much less urine
paragraphs: Urine may become darker and less frequent as drinking decreases and kidney function changes. The care team can explain whether this is expected or whether another cause needs attention.

points.title: Withdrawing from people and surroundings
paragraphs: Someone may speak less, lose interest in usual activities or focus inward. This is not necessarily rejection, anger or depression; quiet presence and familiar voices can still be comforting.

sections.title: What The Final Weeks, Days And Hours May Look Like
sections.intro: Dying does not follow a fixed countdown. Changes can appear gradually, come and go, or happen quickly depending on the illness and the person.

points.title: Weeks before death can look different for everyone
paragraphs: Increasing tiredness, weakness, reduced appetite and needing more help with daily tasks may develop over weeks. These changes alone cannot prove that death is imminent.

points.title: Daily activities often become harder
paragraphs: Washing, dressing, walking and using the toilet may require assistance. Equipment, community nursing and hospice support can reduce strain and help preserve dignity.

points.title: Food and fluid usually reduce gradually
paragraphs: The body needs and processes less nutrition as death approaches. Comfort-focused care usually follows the person's cues instead of setting food or drink targets designed for recovery.

points.title: Wakeful periods may become shorter
paragraphs: Conversation can become brief, delayed or tiring. A person may have a temporary period of clarity, but this does not necessarily mean the underlying condition has reversed.

points.title: Medicines may need a different route
paragraphs: When swallowing becomes difficult, clinicians can use liquids, patches, injections or a syringe driver where appropriate. Do not crush tablets or change doses without professional advice.

points.title: Breathing patterns may change over hours or days
paragraphs: Shallow breaths, deeper rapid breaths and pauses can occur. The rhythm may change repeatedly, and noisy secretions may appear near the end.

points.title: Circulation gradually slows
paragraphs: Blood pressure often falls, the pulse may become weak or irregular, and the extremities can cool or change colour. Blankets can provide comfort, but avoid heating pads that may burn fragile skin.

points.title: Awareness may be limited but hearing may remain
paragraphs: A person who cannot speak or open their eyes may still find a calm voice, gentle touch or familiar music reassuring. Speak naturally and avoid discussing distressing matters as though they are absent.

points.title: The last breaths may be far apart
paragraphs: Near death, breaths may become separated by longer pauses. There can occasionally be one or two reflex breaths after what seemed to be the final breath.

points.title: Only the care team can interpret the whole picture
paragraphs: Clinicians consider the illness, repeated observations, responsiveness, breathing, circulation, urine output and other changes together. Even experienced teams cannot always give an exact time.

next.title: What Do Families Often Notice Near The End?
next.copy: Breathing, awareness and circulation can change in ways that are unfamiliar and difficult to witness.

sections.title: What The Final Hours Of Life May Look Like
sections.intro: These changes are common in expected dying, but every person is different. Contact the care team whenever symptoms seem distressing, medicines cannot be given or the family is unsure what to do.

points.title: Responsiveness may reduce
paragraphs: The person may stop opening their eyes or answering, although hearing may still remain. Speak calmly, explain who is present and avoid assuming they cannot hear.

points.title: Breathing may become irregular
paragraphs: Shallow breaths can alternate with deeper, faster breathing and long pauses. The rhythm may change repeatedly over minutes or hours.

points.title: Breathing can become noisy
paragraphs: Mucus may collect because the person is too weak to cough or swallow. The sound can distress families more than the person; repositioning or prescribed medicine may help.

points.title: Hands and feet may become cool
paragraphs: Circulation slows and skin can become pale, blue or mottled. Use light blankets for comfort and avoid direct heat on fragile skin.

points.title: Urine may become very limited
paragraphs: As fluid intake and kidney function reduce, urine can become darker and much less frequent. The care team can explain whether this fits the expected pattern.

points.title: Restlessness can appear
paragraphs: Picking at bedding, calling out or trying to rise can be caused by pain, a full bladder, medicines, infection or chemical changes. Ask the team to assess distress rather than restraining the person.

points.title: The jaw and face may relax
paragraphs: The mouth may fall open and facial muscles can look different as consciousness and muscle tone reduce. Gentle mouth care can ease dryness.

points.title: The pulse and circulation weaken
paragraphs: The pulse may become faster, slower or irregular and blood pressure usually falls. These measurements are interpreted alongside the person's comfort and overall plan.

points.title: The final breaths may be far apart
paragraphs: Pauses often lengthen before breathing stops. One or two reflex breaths can occasionally occur after what seemed to be the final breath.

points.title: Sudden collapse without an expected-death plan is different
paragraphs: If the person was not expected to die, call emergency services for unresponsiveness, severe breathing difficulty, chest pain, stroke signs, heavy bleeding or a seizure. Do not assume a sudden emergency is part of natural dying.

next.title: What Can Families Do For Comfort?
next.copy: Ten gentle actions can support comfort and dignity without forcing food, fluid or conversation.

sections.title: 10 Ways To Comfort Someone Near The End Of Life
sections.intro: Comfort care should follow the person's wishes and the plan agreed with their healthcare team. Small, calm actions often matter more than trying to correct every change.

points.title: Keep talking in a familiar voice
paragraphs: Introduce yourself, explain what you are doing and share ordinary memories. Hearing may continue after someone can no longer respond, and a calm voice can provide reassurance.

points.title: Follow their lead on touch
paragraphs: Holding a hand, gently stroking an arm or sitting nearby may feel comforting. Stop if the person appears tense or uncomfortable, and respect cultural and personal preferences.

points.title: Offer mouth and lip care
paragraphs: Dryness can be eased with the products and techniques recommended by the care team. If swallowing is unsafe, moistening the mouth may be more comfortable than offering a drink.

points.title: Do not force food or fluid
paragraphs: Pressure to eat can cause distress, nausea or choking when the body no longer wants or manages food. Offer only what is wanted and safe under the care plan.

points.title: Adjust position gently
paragraphs: Pillows and careful repositioning may ease pressure, breathlessness or noisy secretions. Ask nurses how often and how to move the person without causing pain or injury.

points.title: Keep the room calm
paragraphs: Reduce harsh lighting, sudden noise and too many conversations at once. Familiar music, photographs, scents or a quiet open window may help if the person previously enjoyed them.

points.title: Use prescribed comfort medicines correctly
paragraphs: Follow the written plan for pain, breathlessness, nausea, agitation or secretions. Contact the team if a medicine is unavailable, cannot be swallowed or does not appear to help.

points.title: Protect dignity and privacy
paragraphs: Explain personal care, cover the body appropriately and limit visitors when needed. Continue treating the person as an adult with preferences, even when they cannot communicate.

points.title: Include spiritual or cultural wishes
paragraphs: Prayer, music, rituals, silence or contact with a faith or community leader may be important. Ask rather than assume, and tell the care team about practices the family wants respected.

points.title: Let carers rest without guilt
paragraphs: Families cannot watch continuously. Arrange shifts, accept practical help and sleep when possible. Stepping away briefly does not mean abandoning the person.

next.title: What Happens After An Expected Death?
next.copy: Knowing who to call, what can wait and which wishes should be respected can make an overwhelming moment less uncertain.

sections.title: What Families May Need To Know After An Expected Death
sections.intro: Procedures vary by country and place of care. Follow the written plan from the hospice, nurse, doctor or care home and allow time for personal, cultural and religious wishes.

points.title: Pause if you need to
paragraphs: After an expected death there is usually no need to rush immediately. Families may sit quietly, contact someone close or observe a meaningful ritual while following professional guidance.

points.title: Use the number in the care plan
paragraphs: Call the community nurse, hospice, GP, care home or other designated service. They can explain who will verify the death and what happens next.

points.title: Do not call emergency services automatically for an expected death
paragraphs: The agreed plan normally identifies the correct service. If the death was unexpected, circumstances are unclear or there is no plan, use urgent or emergency guidance for your area.

points.title: A qualified professional verifies the death
paragraphs: Verification records that death has occurred. Certification and registration are separate legal steps and their timing depends on the location and circumstances.

points.title: The doctor or medical examiner handles certification
paragraphs: Local procedures determine who completes the medical certificate and whether another authority must review the death. The professional team will explain any delay or referral.

points.title: Contacting a funeral director can usually wait
paragraphs: Once the appropriate professional has advised you, a chosen funeral director can arrange transfer and explain practical options. There is no need to select one through an unsolicited caller.

points.title: Tell professionals about cultural or religious timing
paragraphs: Washing, touching, positioning, prayers, rapid burial or who may be present can matter greatly. Raise these wishes early so they can be respected where law and circumstances allow.

points.title: Registration and official notifications follow
paragraphs: The registrar or local authority explains documents, deadlines and copies of the death certificate. Government services may offer a way to notify several departments together.

points.title: Children and vulnerable adults may need clear support
paragraphs: Use honest, age-appropriate language and a trusted adult. Hospice and bereavement organisations can provide resources tailored to the family.

points.title: Bereavement support is available
paragraphs: Grief can include shock, numbness, relief, anger and exhaustion. Contact a GP, hospice or bereavement service if distress becomes unmanageable or there are concerns about safety.

conclusion.copy: Expected dying should be supported by an individual care plan and a reachable professional team. Families do not have to identify every change or manage difficult symptoms alone.
